articles.title: Peregrinos desaparecidos em avalanche iam para 'montanha proibida' | G1
articles.standfirst: Monte Kailash, no Tibete, é considerado a morada do deus Shiva e é considerado sagrado também por seguidores do budismo, do jainismo e da religião bon. A China veta a presença de escaladores no local.
articles.summary: Monte Kailash, no Tibete, é considerado a morada do deus Shiva e é considerado sagrado também por seguidores do budismo, do jainismo e da religião bon.
articles.body:
O Monte Kailash, com mais de 6 mil metros de altura, é considerado um lugar sagrado — Foto: QuartierLatin1968/Creative Commons

Entre os 517 estrangeiros desaparecidos na avalanche que atingiu o Nepal e o Tibete na quarta-feira (24) , a grande maioria é de indianos.

Boa parte deles estava na região para uma peregrinação religiosa que atrai milhares de seguidores do hinduísmo: a ida ao Monte Kailash , considerado a morada de Shiva e outros deuses da religião.

O Monte Kailash é uma montanha localizada no Tibete, a cerca de 100 km da fronteira entre a China e o Nepal. Seu pico fica 6.638 metros acima do nível do mar.

Apesar de ter havido tentativas de escalada nas décadas de 1920 e 1930, não há nenhum registro de chegada ao topo da montanha na história. A China, onde o Monte Kailash fica atualmente, proíbe qualquer tentativa de escalada, em respeito ao significado religioso do local.

Uma das rotas de peregrinação inclui a passagem pelo Nepal, em áreas afetadas pela avalanche. Os viajantes seguem até Rasuwa e cruzam a fronteira entre Nepal e China pelo posto de Rasuwagadhi. Do outro lado da fronteira fica a região de Gyirong de onde a viagem continua em direção ao Monte Kailash.

Ao "New York Times", um iogue indiano conhecido como Sadhguru afirmou que 77 integrantes de grupos organizados por sua fundação estavam no centro de imigração da fronteira entre Nepal e Tibete quando a inundação atingiu o local. Até o momento, ele ainda não conseguiu contato com o grupo.

As escrituras hinduístas associam o Kailash com diversos deuses. No épico Ramayana, que circula na Índia antiga desde o século V a.C., a montanha aparece como residência do deus Shiva, de sua mulher, Parvati, e de seus filhos, como Ganesha, o deus com cabeça de elefante.

Algumas tradições identificam o local com a nascente espiritual do rio Ganges e com o Monte Meru, o centro do universo.

Seguidores da religião fazem peregrinações à montanha e também ao lago Manasarovar , a cerca de 35 km do pé da montanha, também com conotações sagradas.

Imagem de drone mostra devastação em Trishuli, no Nepal, após avalanche de lama — Foto: Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters

O Monte Kailash e o lago também são considerados sagrados para outras religiões: o budismo tibetano , o jainismo e a religião bon , culto praticado no Tibete.

Para os budistas, a montanha também é a manifestação física do Monte Meru, além de local de meditação de um antigo mestre chamado Milarepa, do século XI d.C. Já os seguidores do bon acreditam que o topo do monte é a morada de 360 deuses.

O jainismo, que é uma religião indiana centrada na não violência, acredita, por sua vez, que o monte Kailash é o local onde o primeiro dos 24 "salvadores" conseguiu se libertar do ciclo de mortes e reencarnações.

Infográfico mostra local da avalanche de lama no Nepal e no Tibete — Foto: Editoria de Arte/g1

articles.title: Sertanejo Felipe emagrece 65 kg e revela motivação pelos filhos | G1
articles.standfirst: Cantor contou ao g1 em Barretos que mudança vai além da aparência e representa uma nova conduta para a vida. Pai de duas crianças pequenas, ele diz que quer estar presente pelo maior tempo possível.
articles.summary: O sertanejo Felipe, da dupla com Rodrigo, detalha como a paternidade o motivou a perder 65 kg para garantir mais saúde e tempo de vida ao lado dos filhos pequenos.
articles.body:
Ser o melhor pai possível e acompanhar o crescimento dos filhos pelo maior tempo que conseguir. Foi pensando em Bento, de 2 anos, e Benício, de 9 meses, que Felipe, da dupla com Rodrigo, decidiu mudar a própria rotina e cuidar mais da saúde. O resultado aparece na balança: o cantor perdeu 65 quilos.

"Acho que foi muito pelos meus filhos também. Eu tenho o Bentinho, de 2 anos, e o Benício, com 9 meses. Vai fazer um ano agora. [...] Nossos filhos são o maior bem da nossa vida. Então eu quero ser o melhor pai possível, pelo maior tempo que eu conseguir."

Em entrevista ao g1 durante a Festa do Peão de Barretos 2026 , Felipe contou que ainda está em processo de emagrecimento e que a transformação representa uma nova forma de encarar a vida, muito além da mudança física.

"Já foram 65 kg. [...] Acho que é um negócio mais para a saúde, para a vida mesmo. Foi a melhor experiência que eu tive na minha vida, perder esse peso, porque hoje eu sou outra pessoa."

A mudança acontece em um momento importante também na carreira. Felipe e Rodrigo se preparam para gravar, em setembro, em Brasília (DF), o maior projeto audiovisual da trajetória da dupla.

Para o cantor, porém, chegar mais magro à gravação é apenas parte de uma decisão com objetivos muito mais duradouros.

O sertanejo Felipe em 2025, no palco da Festa do Peão de Barretos, e em 2026, após emagrecer 65 kg — Foto: Ricardo Nasi e Vitor Chaves

Ao falar sobre o processo de emagrecimento, Felipe contou que recebeu ajuda e conselhos de amigos. Entre eles, citou Henrique, da dupla Henrique & Juliano.

O sertanejo também atribui o resultado à determinação em manter a decisão que tomou.

"Eu sou uma pessoa muito decidida. Quando eu decido um negócio, eu bato muito firme na tecla mesmo."

Com dois filhos ainda pequenos, a paternidade ganhou peso especial nessa escolha. Ao explicar o que espera conquistar com a mudança, Felipe voltou a falar sobre tempo e qualidade de vida.

"Quero ser o melhor pai possível, pelo maior tempo que eu conseguir. [...] É o que vai fazer, pelo menos, eu tentar viver o máximo possível."

articles.title: Paula Fernandes em Barretos: Cantora fala de machismo e carreira | G1
articles.standfirst: Cantora retorna à Festa do Peão de Barretos, o maior rodeio da América Latina, na noite desta quinta-feira (27), depois de dez anos afastada do evento.
articles.summary: Paula Fernandes celebra retorno à Festa do Peão de Barretos e comenta os desafios das mulheres no sertanejo e sua posição contra a IA na música.
articles.body:
A cantora Paula Fernandes — Foto: Divulgação

Será em cima de um cavalo, cantando Ave Maria , que Paula Fernandes retorna à Festa do Peão de Barretos, o maior rodeio da América Latina, na noite desta quinta-feira (27/8), depois de dez anos afastada do evento. A apresentação dará início às provas de montaria, que antecedem os shows musicais.

A cantora retorna na sexta-feira (28/8) para uma apresentação só sua, no palco Amanhecer, um dos principais do evento. O show — que reúne seus primeiros sucessos, como Pássaro de Fogo , e músicas de seu novo álbum, 30 & Poucos Anos — marcará também a comemoração de seus 42 anos e será uma oportunidade de revisitar sua carreira.

Em entrevista à BBC News Brasil por videoconferência, ela relembrou sua trajetória, desde a infância pobre no interior de Minas Gerais até o início da carreira, cantando em botecos, e a chegada ao estrelato em 2011, quando foi a artista mais tocada do ano nas rádios e vendeu 1,6 milhão de discos pelo país.

Paula diz que a principal diferença que sente hoje é que a indústria já está acostumada à presença de mulheres no sertanejo — um cenário muito diferente daquele que encontrou no início da carreira, quando chegou a fazer 220 shows no ano.

"Não consigo descrever o olhar de espanto de quando eu chegava. 'Por que ela pediu um banheiro no camarim? Por que pediu um espelho?'. Era tudo moldado para homens, que chegam de botina, trocam de roupa em qualquer lugar, colocam uma camisa xadrez, fazem xixi em qualquer lugar", conta. "A gente pede um palco sem buracos, porque uso salto, e isso são necessidades femininas, não luxo."

Paula diz que, embora possa "parecer repetitiva", não se cansa de falar sobre isso porque, ainda hoje, após a criação do movimento feminejo e o sucesso de nomes como Marília Mendonça, as mulheres ainda são minoria no sertanejo.

Detalhe da capa do disco 30 & Poucos Anos, de Paula Fernandes, que retoma um de seus principais sucessos, Pássaro de Fogo — Foto: Divulgação

Prova disso é o line-up da sexta-feira em Barretos, quando ela cantará. Entre os 22 artistas que subirão aos palcos, apenas três são mulheres, ou seja, 13,6%. A proporção é ainda menor quando considerada a programação completa do evento: as mulheres representam 11,6% das atrações dos seis dias.

A artista celebra, no entanto, que os nomes da nova geração, como Ana Castela, não tenham de enfrentar o que ela enfrentou, como as fofocas de que teve sua carreira impulsionada por supostos affairs com homens da indústria musical.

"Me deram cinco namorados em uma semana. Aí a frase era: 'boazinha, mas passa o rodo, né?'. E eu solteira, super quietinha", relembra.

Na conversa com a BBC, a artista ainda falou sobre o sucesso — e as críticas — de suas versões em português de sucessos estrangeiros, como Shallow, de Lady Gaga; os novos rumos do sertanejo, que agora incorpora até batidas de funk; por que prefere se resguardar quando o assunto é política; e seus novos trabalhos.

Além do disco 30 & Poucos Anos , que tem o single Era Eu , ela fará uma série de shows por casas de espetáculos, cujas datas serão anunciadas em breve.

BBC News Brasil — Você vai voltar à arena da Festa do Peão cantando Ave Maria montada a cavalo, algo que fazia no início de sua carreira. De onde veio essa tradição?

Paula Fernandes — Eu ganhei a vida com Ave Maria. Colocou comida na minha mesa desde que me entendo por gente. Sempre cantei em abertura de rodeio, e Ave Maria é um momento importante. É quando os peões fazem uma oração de proteção, porque [a montaria] é um esporte arriscado.

Às vezes eu entrava a pé, às vezes faziam um coração de fogo ao meu redor. Isso é uma memória afetiva tão boa, porque colocava comida na minha mesa e prazeroso, poder orar pelos peões.

BBC News Brasil — Você está comemorando 30 anos de estrada e, quando estourou, nem se falava em feminejo. Você se considera precursora do movimento?

Paula — Eu fui uma das, mas antes existiram — e existem ainda — Sula Miranda, Roberta Miranda, as irmãs Galvão, as Marcianas. Naquela época era mais difícil do que quando eu aconteci, mas sinto orgulho de estar contribuindo na pavimentação de uma estrada difícil contra o preconceito contra as mulheres na música, ainda mais em um meio dominado por duplas masculinas.

A gente tem que levantar essa bandeira. Posso parecer repetitiva, mas a gente ainda precisa de mais espaço nas grades de shows dos grandes eventos, para ter um equilíbrio com os meninos. Não queremos o espaço de ninguém, mas também merecemos o nosso.

BBC News Brasil — Houve todas essas que você citou, mas, naquele momento, em que elas não estavam no auge, você se sentia sozinha?

Paula — Completamente. Não consigo descrever o olhar de espanto de quando eu chegava, porque ser uma dama nesse meio é diferente. Existia um espanto, uma curiosidade, e ao mesmo tempo uma rejeição. 'Quem é essa mulher? Por que ela pediu um banheiro no camarim? Por que pediu um espelho?'. Era tudo moldado para homens, que chegam de botina, trocam de roupa em qualquer lugar, colocam uma camisa xadrez e está tudo certo, faz xixi em qualquer lugar.

Acaba que a gente precisa de mais cuidado. A gente pede um palco sem buracos, porque uso salto, e isso são necessidades femininas, não luxo. Eu sentia essa resistência. 'Mas fulano veio aqui ontem e não pediu isso.' Mas eu sou uma dama! A coisa foi evoluindo, e isso se tornou uma prática mais comum, receber uma menina e saber que é diferente.

BBC News Brasil — Naquela época você sofria muitas críticas. Diziam que 'a Paula é chata'.

Paula — Foi um susto, e eu compreendo que era novo. A vida da mulher na estrada é muito mais difícil, a gente precisa de tempo para se maquiar, a mulher tem TPM, às vezes deixa o filho em casa, então rolou isso, sim.

BBC News Brasil — Diziam inclusive que você tinha affairs na indústria que teriam impulsionado sua carreira, né?

Paula — Me deram cinco namorados em uma semana. Aí a frase era: 'boazinha, mas passa o rodo, né?'. E eu solteira, super quietinha. Sempre tive a conduta de ser muito correta e ir de casa para o trabalho, do trabalho para casa. No meio eu não namorei praticamente ninguém, então de certa forma isso incomodava um pouco. 'Como uma artista não é namoradeira? Ela tem que ser alguma coisa, então vamos dar um rótulo para ela.' E eu sempre fui uma máquina de trabalho.

Mas faz parte: quando a gente está em cima do palco, existem muitos tipos de olhares. Mesmo diante disso tudo, fui muito feliz. E hoje sou mais ainda.

BBC News Brasil — Quando você desacelerou o ritmo de shows, teve medo de te esquecerem?

Paula — A vida é feita de ciclos. Cheguei a fazer 220 apresentações no ano em 2011. Realmente é muito cansativo, dá muito trabalho chegar até as pessoas, mas eu sempre fiz com tanto amor que valia a pena quando encontrava aquela multidão. Com o tempo, o cansaço bate e a gente vai entendendo que a gente não fica no pico a vida inteira.

O que tem depois do céu? Porque eu alcancei o céu, então o que eu mais desejava era atingir a velocidade de cruzeiro. Era humanamente impossível manter aquela rotina. Eu precisava da minha casa, da minha cama, dos meus bichos, de tempo para ser uma pessoa normal.

Eu fui conseguindo essa rotina até chegar neste momento, em que tenho tempo de ter a minha vida pessoal, constituir família e até ter espaço para ouvir meu silêncio e compor. Foi muito legal, eu faria tudo de novo, mas acho que meu maior sucesso estou vivendo agora. Equilíbrio é sinônimo de sucesso para mim.

BBC News Brasil — O cansaço te deprimia?

Paula — Deprimida não. Eu fiquei deprimida na adolescência, aos 18 anos, me tratei, mas naquela época fiquei muito cansada. A gente fica mais impaciente, mais ansioso, a gente deseja a cama da gente. Mas sempre me saí muito bem.

BBC News Brasil — Outra coisa que marcou sua carreira foram as versões em português de sucessos estrangeiros. Pretende continuar fazendo?

Paula — Eu tinha aversão a isso. Para mim, era um crime pegar uma música tão perfeita e adaptar, mas acabei me tornando uma grande versionista. É um desafio foda, uma Adele liberar uma canção para eu fazer em português, então mudei minha forma de pensar. Pretendo, sim, continuar fazendo, e acaba caindo no meu colo.

BBC News Brasil — Essas versões envolvem a expectativa dos fãs. Ora você foi muito celebrada, ora não gostaram tanto. Como você lidou com as críticas quando fez Shallow?

Paula — Mas elas não gostaram? Eu não soube. O que vi foi virar meme por causa do 'juntos e shallow now'. Acabou virando marketing. Nem nos meus melhores sonhos eu poderia imaginar que isso viraria um marketing que até o McDonald's usaria.

Eu não vi como não gostar. Vi como algo que gerou curiosidade, e o povo gosta de um meme. Eu mesmo fiz alguns. Isso para mim foi confortável, engajou, tanto que no Spotify é uma das minhas músicas mais ouvidas. A gente podia ter feito a melhor estratégia que não ia alcançar isso, então achei muito positivo.

Os implicantes iam implicar de qualquer forma, mas faz parte. Quando você está lá em cima, vai ter gente que vai tacar pedra e vai ter gente que vai aplaudir. Mas o saldo foi positivo.

É engraçado, porque tem tantas músicas que tem trechinhos em inglês, 'eu perguntava do you wanna dance', o próprio Luan [Santana] lançou algo que falava que ele estava na bad. Pode ter tido uma implicanciazinha, mas para mim foi muito bom.

BBC News Brasil — Hoje muitas adaptações para o português estão sendo feitas com inteligência artificial. Você usa IA no seu trabalho?

Paula — Me nego. Como criadora, é inadmissível usar uma vírgula do Chat. É um crime contra minha natureza, porque sou uma criadora desde que me entendo por gente.

A IA, sendo bem usada, é maravilhoso, mas para essa parte eu me questiono o que vai ser dos compositores. Como eles vão provar que aquilo saiu deles? Seja da cabeça, seja do coração. Para mim, sempre foi do coração. Quando componho com sentimento, sinto que toco as pessoas, então é inconcebível, porque não vai tocar do mesmo jeito. Para emocionar, tem que ser humano, vulnerável, profundo. E IA não tem profundidade, entende?

Outra coisa: tem que haver uma legalização de direitos autorais, porque fica muito fácil, colocar 'quero compor uma música igual à da Paula Fernandes'. O que é meu é meu. Se você não gostar, é minha culpa; se gostar, é minha conquista.

BBC News Brasil — Às vésperas das eleições, como você se posiciona em relação à política? A festa de Barretos, aliás, é um lugar onde os artistas se posicionam muito.

Paula — Eu lido com isso com muita tranquilidade, já que sempre fui apartidária. Eu sou uma representante da poesia, da arte, e a arte é universal, chega e alcança pessoas de todas as etnias, raças, cores, àquele que não tem e àquele que tem muito, então acho que seria muito leviano entrar numa área que não é da minha alçada. Eu não entendo disso.

Todo mundo tem sua filosofia, aquilo que acredita mais, mas minha arte alcança todos igualmente. Eu não me sinto apta a fazer isso. Não me sinto confortável a fazer isso. Na hora do meu voto, ele é meu voto, eu tenho direito a ter meu voto e ser algo íntimo meu, que vou guardar para mim, senão todo mundo saia dizendo 'acabei de votar e...', entendeu?

Eu prefiro estar nesse lugar de representante de alguém que faz algo que alcança todos. Mas desejo que as pessoas pensem com carinho, façam suas próprias avaliações, questionem seus candidatos e escolham o que é melhor para si, com sua intuição e seu livre-arbítrio.

Eu não posso abrir mão do meu livre-arbítrio e também não posso interferir no do outro. Eu não tenho esse direito, então prefiro me posicionar dessa forma. Eu sei daquilo que julgo combinar mais com a minha filosofia, sabe? Vou guardar para mim. Acho que tenho esse direito.

BBC News Brasil — O sertanejo tem incorporado outros gêneros musicais como o funk. Você trabalha muito com a tradição, mas como você vê essa renovação?

Paula — Eu acho tudo muito rico. Gosto de música independente do gênero. Não vejo problema em colocar um beat de funk numa canção ou trazer alguém do samba e do pagode para cantar junto. Eu sou uma representante da música popular brasileira, minha essência e minha raíz é sertaneja, mas nunca me rotulei nem me limitei a nenhum gênero.

A gente não tem mais que ficar apegada ao padrão. Eu não sou uma pessoa padrão, uma artista padrão. A gente tem que ser genuíno, e o que faz diferença, até para os artistas que estão chegando, é não copiar ninguém. Agora, no álbum 30 & Poucos Anos, pude trazer a roupagem mais country, que é algo de que sempre gostei, assim como a música folk, mas naquela época me tolhiam, diziam que não era brasileiro, que não traria brasilidade. Mas, gente, isso é música.

E eu sou da mensagem. É uma coisa que eu questiono, sim. Acho que todo mundo tem a liberdade de fazer o que quiser, mas eu tenho responsabilidade com o que canto, com o que falo, porque sei que sou uma referência para muita gente que está me escutando, e a palavra tem muito poder.

BBC News Brasil — O que mudou na sua forma de compor, comparando a Paula de 2011, que fazia 220 shows por ano, e a de agora?

Paula — Minha vivência mudou. Eu era uma menina anônima, sem grana, que não tinha nem onde morar direito, não tinha o que comer direito, passava todo tipo de necessidade, e fui retratando, à medida que o tempo foi passando, minhas vivências. A gente passa a ter uma forma diferente de se expressar, mas a essência não muda.

BBC News Brasil — Muita gente nas redes sociais duvida da sua infância humilde, acredita?

Paula — Não sei se é pior quem inventa ou quem acredita. Se eu puder fazer um resumo da minha vida, eu sou uma das poucas mulheres que conheço que nasceu e cresceu num lugar que não tinha luz elétrica, não tinha nem privada no banheiro. Só depois de muito tempo que chegou a energia elétrica. Eu passava 30 dias sem ver ninguém além da minha família. Vivi nesse lugar muito tempo até ir para a cidade estudar.

Foi a melhor infância do mundo: montava a cavalo, vivia o dia inteiro descalça, tinha uma colônia de bichos-de-pé nos dedos, meu cabelo vivia cheio de gravetos, era um inferno para desembaraçar. Eu era um menino, de botina, de calça jeans.

Mas fui paupérrima. A gente produzia o que a gente comia e ia para cidade comprar arroz e sal. Fico tentando entender o que faz as pessoas inventarem essas coisas, porque é inacreditável. Eu sou filha da roça. E continuo sendo. A diferença é que moro num lugar bonito, mas não tem nada bordado a ouro, nada assinado por designer. E tudo o que tenho é fruto da minha dignidade — e da minha mãe, que é uma leoa.

BBC News Brasil — Qual foi o papel da sua mãe na sua carreira, aliás?

Paula — Se não fosse por ela, eu tinha pulado aquela janela. Com 18 anos, eu escolhi uma janela para pular, e minha mãe falou 'se você pular, eu vou pular antes'. Minha mãe me salvou milhões de vezes.

Foi ela que acreditou no meu sonho. Ela foi a primeira pessoa que me viu cantar. Ela que não duvidou. Ela que [me ouvia quando] eu chegava em casa, depois de tocar de terça a domingo em botecos para ganhar R$ 40, e falava 'mãe, será que vai acontecer algum dia para mim ou vou ser caixa de som a vida inteira'? Ela dizia 'Paula, você vai ser uma das maiores artistas do Brasil', e olha onde minha música chegou.

Talvez eu seja real demais, e não sei se as pessoas estão preparadas. Vão continuar falando um monte de coisas, mas não vou mudar. Passei por muita dificuldade, por muita coisa, só não passei fome por causa da minha mãe. Mas superei tudo e estou aqui. Se é para motivar as pessoas, gente, todo mundo tem problema, mas o importante é saber que sempre tem o dia seguinte e a gente consegue se superar. Acho muito legal ter esse papo, porque estou aqui para falar de música, mas é muito bom imaginar que posso agregar algum valor à vida de alguém.

articles.title: At least 12 dead as wildfires sweep through northern Algeria
articles.summary: Northern Africa has experienced severe heatwaves this summer, leading to hundreds of fires across the region.
articles.body:
At least 12 people have been killed and dozens injured as wildfires burn through large swathes of northern Algeria.

Civil protection authorities said dozens of blazes swept through several provinces along the country's northern coastline.

At least 54 people had suffered burn injuries, with at least six of them being treated in intensive care, Interior Minister Said Sayoud said on Wednesday night.

The deaths comes as northern Africa swelters under a severe heatwave, with Tunisia and Algeria particularly affected.

Sayoud said five people were killed in Jijel province, four in Bejaia and three in Tizi Ouzou.

He has travelled to Bejaia with the Algerian Health Minister Mohamed Seddik Ait Messaoudene to "assess" local firefighting and evacuation efforts, government officials said.

Many homes in Bejaia and Jijel have been evacuated, according to the civil protection agency and local media.

Footage shared by local broadcaster Jijel News showed residents taking refuge in a post office as thick clouds of smoke billowed around them.

Firefighters were battling 69 blazes across the country, the civil protection agency said earlier on Wednesday evening.

The Bejaia region saw devastating fires tear through forest and farmland three years ago when 30 people were killed.

Last month, the authorities recorded at least six deaths caused by fires, with crews battling more than 2,000 blazes across Algeria in July alone.

While Algeria regularly experiences forest fires around the summer months, climate change has exacerbated the intensity and severity of recent wildfires in the country.

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said extreme heat had become common in North Africa, a region that has seen the most rapid warming of the six subregions of Africa - 0.43C per decade - between 1991 and 2025.

Rising heat and water shortages have also led to an increase in camel deaths during summer heatwaves in Algeria, a recent study revealed.

articles.title: Samay Raina felicitated by CM Fadnavis at Mumbai event: 'Mera aur cyber cell ka rishta bahut purana hai'
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Maharashtra Cyber launched a cyber-awareness short film, Digital Arrest, and the 1930 Maharashtra Cyber Anthem at an event in Mumbai on Wednes.
articles.body: MUMBAI: Maharashtra Cyber launched a cyber-awareness short film, Digital Arrest, and the 1930 Maharashtra Cyber Anthem at an event in Mumbai on Wednesday, attended by several celebrities and Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis.Actors Ashish Vidyarthi, Pankaj Tripathi, Sharad Kelkar, Sonali Bendre, Javed Jaffrey and Mangesh Desai, along with singer Sunidhi Chauhan and comedian Samay Raina, were among those who contributed to the campaign and attended the event.Speaking at the event, Fadnavis stressed the importance of public awareness in tackling cybercrime. He said artists, actors and singers could play an important role in reaching citizens with messages about online fraud.“Cyber criminals dupe citizens by frightening and intimidating them in the name of police, the CBI, or judges. Citizens must not fall prey to any such tactics and should immediately contact the cyber helpline number ‘1930’ in case of cyber fraud,” Fadnavis said.The celebrities were felicitated for their contribution to the Digital Arrest short film and the 1930 Maharashtra Cyber Anthem.Samay Raina, who was also felicitated, spoke about his long association with Maharashtra Cyber.“Thank you so much for the felicitation. Mera aur Maharashtra cell ka rishta bahut purana hai. (My relationship with the Maharashtra Cyber cell is very old. Bahut zyada active hai Maharashtra cyber cell (Maharashtra Cyber is very active), wherever you are, US or India, they will catch you,” he said.Speaking from personal experience, Raina said, “1930 is really a great number. I have actually saved it because I often get calls from there.”He then joked about being woken up in the morning for the event.“This is the first time the Cyber Cell has woken a comedian in the morning to felicitate someone,” Raina said.Speaking to ANI, Ashish Vidyarthi said the campaign was important because technology, while making people's lives easier, was also being used by criminals to target ordinary citizens.“I feel that we all use technology to make our lives easier, and people use it to destroy the lives of ordinary people. I think this campaign is important so that you stop this crime from happening,” he said.“It’s important to spread awareness that there is no such thing as digital arrest. The films that are being made, the apps that are being announced, that is such a wonderful thing. People will finally know about the ongoing big scam,” he added.The campaign seeks to raise awareness about the so-called “digital arrest” scam, in which fraudsters impersonate police officers, government officials or other authorities to frighten victims and extort money from them.Fadnavis urged citizens to remain alert and contact the 1930 cyber helpline immediately if they fall victim to cyber fraud.(With inputs from ANI)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: Khalid Sheikh Mohammed: Trial date set for alleged 9/11 mastermind
articles.summary: His plea deal to avoid a death-penalty trial was rejected by a federal appeals court last summer.
articles.body:
Alleged 9/11 terror attacks mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed will stand trial in June 2028, more than a quarter of a century after what the US government has called "the most egregious criminal act on American soil in modern history".

A military judge ruled the trial would start in two years because a 2027 date sought by prosecutors was too soon.

Mohammed had reached a plea deal where he would admit guilt in exchange for avoiding a death-penalty trial, but a federal appeals court threw out the agreement last summer. Arrested in 2003, he has been held at Guantanamo Bay since September 2006.

Mohammed has previously said he planned 2001's "9/11 operation from A-to-Z".

US Air Force judge Lt Col Michael A Schrama ruled on Wednesday that the trial for Mohammed and three co-accused would start on 5 June, 2028.

Alleged accomplices Walid bin Attash, Ali Abdul Aziz Ali and Mustafa al-Hawsawi were listed in the court document.

The start date allowed for additional time to deal with matters of the court, such as resolving any disputes about what evidence can be presented, the judge wrote.

Next month will mark 25 years since hijackers flew planes into the World Trade Center in New York City and the Pentagon in Virginia, while another flight they hijacked crashed in a field in Pennsylvania. About 3,000 people died in the attacks.

Mohammed is accused of conceiving the idea of training pilots to fly commercial planes into buildings and taking those plans to Osama Bin Laden, leader of al-Qaeda.

Mohammed, a US-educated engineer, was captured along with al-Hawsawi in Pakistan in March 2003.

The rejected plea deal, which would have given Mohammed a life sentence without possibility of parole, was reached after two years of negotiation and signed by an official appointed by then-Defence Secretary Lloyd Austin.

But Austin was reportedly caught by surprise, and immediately attempted to revoke it.

The military prison in Guantanamo Bay opened six months after the attacks.

About 15 prisoners are still detained there.

articles.title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu's advice to engineers entering business: Learn to sell, face rejection
articles.summary: Tech News News: Moving from engineering, medicine or science into business can require learning a skill that many professionals may not encounter in their regular wor.
articles.body: Moving from engineering, medicine or science into business can require learning a skill that many professionals may not encounter in their regular work: selling. In an X (formerly Twitter) post, Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu shared a simple piece of advice for engineers, scientists and doctors who want to enter the business world—go on sales calls and learn to deal with rejection. Vembu said that technical knowledge alone is not enough to build a business. He argued that speaking directly with potential customers can help professionals explain their ideas better, understand the value of sales and develop the skills needed to run a business.Sridhar Vembu says business begins with selling“If you are an engineer or scientist or doctor turning to business, the first thing I would suggest is ‘Please go on a lot of sales calls, face rejection if necessary, but persist’,” Sridhar Vembu wrote in the post.According to Vembu, selling can also improve communication skills. People with technical backgrounds may understand their products or ideas deeply, but explaining them to someone else—and convincing that person to pay for them—is a different challenge.“You will develop better communication skills as you realise that explaining your ideas is not so easy,” he said.Sales calls can also change the way professionals view salespeople. Vembu said people who spend time trying to sell a product may develop greater respect for those whose job involves speaking to customers and handling rejection every day.“You will develop respect for sales people. You may even become good at business!” he added.The simple lesson behind Sridhar Vembu's adviceAt the heart of Vembu's post is a basic idea: a business cannot survive without customers and sales.“There is no such thing as a business without selling something. Sometimes the most obvious thing has to be said!” Vembu wrote.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Nepal floods: Aerial views reveal trail of destruction after powerful surge of ice, mud and boulders
articles.summary: South Asia News: Nepal came under the sudden force of a massive flood on Wednesday, leaving a trail of devastation as the Himalayan fury claimed at least 165 lives and.
articles.body: Nepal came under the sudden force of a massive flood on Wednesday, leaving a trail of devastation as the Himalayan fury claimed at least 165 lives and left more than 1300 people missing.The Himalayan nation’s northern region bore the brunt of the disaster, with Rasuwa district on China-Nepal border among the worst-hit areas.The fury was carried by the Bhote Koshi River, which originates in Tibet and came rushing down with enormous force, carrying with it ice, rocks, mud and debris.Also Read: Nepal Floods Live UpdatesThe aftermath offers a stark picture of the destruction left behind. Villages appear wiped out, roads have vanished and entire stretches of civilisation seem to have been swept away by nature’s fury.Nuwakot, barely 50 kilometres and around a two-hour drive from Rasuwa, bears the deadly imprint of the floods. The river appears to have changed course, pushing aside the settlements that once stood along its path and spreading a vast stretch of muddy debris across the landscape.The flood tore through the Sino-Nepalese border region, destroying almost everything in its way, sweeping away vehicles, ripping apart roads and engulfing entire villages in the northern Himalayan region.The debris that ravaged Rasuwa and surrounding areas was a deadly mix of ice, rock and mud that rushed into the Bhote Koshi River, turning it into a torrent of destruction.The scale of the disaster also highlights a wider and growing threat facing the Hindu Kush Himalayas. Floods, landslides, avalanches and droughts are becoming more frequent and severe across the region, while rapid changes to water, land and air are posing a major threat to millions of people, according to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD).The organisation said on Wednesday that the flash flood sent a powerful surge of water, sediment and boulders through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems.In the downstream Galchhi area, water levels in the river reportedly rose by as much as nine metres, nearly 30 feet, in just 30 minutes.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: People's Palace revamp gets £14m government boost
articles.summary: The well-loved Glasgow museum has been closed since 2024 for a major refurbishment.
articles.body:
Long-running efforts to reopen one of Glasgow's most famous museums have received a welcome boost.

The People's Palace closed in April 2024 for a £36m upgrade and the attached Winter Gardens, a large glass conservatory, has been closed since 2019.

It had been hoped the attraction would be back in public use by 2027, but earlier this year the project was delayed indefinitely .

The Scottish government has now announced up to £14m to support the rising refurbishment costs.

Glasgow Life, the charity that runs the city's cultural attractions, said at the start of the year that timelines - as well as cost estimates for the work - were "continuing to evolve" for the Category A listed building which sits on Glasgow Green.

The refurbishment was announced two years ago, with funding from various sources including the National Lottery Heritage Fund and Glasgow City Council.

No Scottish government cash was earmarked for the project at the time and in January, Billy Garrett, the director of culture, tourism and events at Glasgow Life, told a Holyrood committee his organisation was "disappointed" to see there was no government funding for the People's Palace.

This latest investment is in addition to £19.5m of funding contributions from Glasgow City Council, Glasgow Life, and the National Lottery Heritage Fund, with further funding opportunities continuing to be explored to ensure the full refurbishment of the site.

It is hoped the revamp will support jobs and footfall in Glasgow's east end and safeguard historic collections and artefacts that tell Glasgow's story, as well as preserving the attached Winter Gardens for community use.

Culture Secretary Màiri McAllan said People's Palace was a "cherished part" of Glasgow's history and she looked forward to seeing the refurbishment plans progress.

She said: "I am pleased to confirm that the Scottish government has announced up to £14m in conditional support to the refurbishment of the People's Palace and secure its reopening to the public.

"This is about far more than bricks and mortar. The People's Palace has welcomed generations of Glaswegians as well as visitors from further afield, and this investment will ensure they can continue to enjoy it for decades to come."

The conditional support remains subject to a final business case being submitted by Glasgow Life, funding conditions being met in accordance with the Scottish Public Finance Manual and assessment to ensure compliance with the Subsidy Control Act 2022.

The council's culture convener and chair of Glasgow Life, Bailie Annette Christie said the landmark was undergoing a "once-in-a-generation transformation".

She added: "It's a complex and ambitious project that has been co-created with the people of Glasgow and will secure the long-term future of one of the city's most treasured and nationally important cultural spaces.

"We are grateful to the Scottish government for this welcome investment, which is a significant vote of confidence in our plans and brings us an important step closer to creating an inclusive, accessible and world-class social history museum and visitor destination in the city's east end.

"Glasgow has a strong track record of delivering major cultural and heritage developments, and we look forward to continuing to work with the Scottish government and wider partners to deliver a revitalised People's Palace and Winter Gardens."

articles.title: Summer holiday season 'almost 10 out of 10' for Cornwall venue
articles.summary: Holiday park boosted by hot weather but other venues give mixed reports on 2026 summer season.
articles.body:
A holiday park owner has said the weather this summer helped boost bookings in a season that had been "almost 10 out of 10".

Jon Hyatt, of Hendra Holiday Park in Newquay said 2026, had been 'building from January", after quieter years for the industry in 2024 and 2025.

Sally Everton, of tourism organisation Visit Devon, said this year had been a "mixed bag" but coastal holiday locations had benefitted from the sunshine.

The Devon Association of Tourist Attractions said its members had given "mixed reviews" of the year, with some reporting lower visitor numbers as holidaymakers opted for "beach days over attraction days".

Hyatt said it had been a fantastic summer for his holiday park in north Cornwall.

"We've seen strong demand ever since the start of the year but the heatwaves and the increase in staycations has been the cherry on top," he said.

"This summer has got to be close to 10 out of 10 in terms of the weather and the bookings we've seen."

Hyatt said the park had just opened an indoor activity centre which it hoped would boost visitor numbers outside the main holiday season.

The project cost about £3m and was part funded by the government, through the UK Shared Prosperity Fund.

Everton said the 2026 season so far had been "seven out of ten" in Devon.

"We may have had heatwaves but we've also had cost of living pressures, with people being very careful about how they are spending their money," she said.

Everton added families feeling the financial squeeze may have "chosen to go to the beach and take a picnic, rather than spending in cafes".

"Visitors may come for the holiday but it's about what they choose to do when they are here," she added.

Roger Sell, who is managing director of River Dart Country Park near Ashburton, said it had been a brilliant year for the attraction with visitor numbers up on 2025.

"We're up on day visitors, the campsite is up and we're seeing an increase in last minute bookings too," he said.

The park, which has about 70,000 visitors a year, is celebrating its 50th anniversary in 2026.

But Sell, who is also chair of the Devon Association of Tourist Attractions, said other attractions had given "mixed reviews" of the 2026 season.

"Some attractions have slight increases in visitors, some are saying it's slightly down on footfall but nearly all are saying the visitor spend is up."

"It's all been weather related," he said.

articles.summary: New leader has already repainted road markings - but will he be able to lower council taxes?
articles.body:
Before May, he was a businessman who would drive around his home city of Wakefield wishing the potholes could be fixed.

After standing for Reform UK in the local elections, the keen musician found himself the leader of Wakefield Council after his party won 58 of the 63 seats on offer and ended decades of Labour majority rule.

It hasn't all been plain sailing - already two councillors, Steve Lewis and Rhys Carr, have left Reform to sit as independents, and a third, Nick Farmer, has been suspended by the party.

It is now 100 days since the Annual General Meeting when the party were sworn in - but are they delivering the change they promised and that people voted for?

I spent an afternoon in Wakefield city centre with Johnson to find out.

As the ballots were counted on 8 May, Reform in Wakefield didn't have a leader or a deputy.

Johnson was elected to lead the group within days, and 10 days later was leader of the council.

The former rock singer's flowing hair makes him a recognisable figure, and on a walkabout in the city centre, people constantly stop him to chat, thanking him for responding to their emails and talking about the difference they believe Reform are making.

He does have some political experience, having previously served as a Conservative councillor, and says he wants to make Wakefield a better place for all.

"I used to drive through the streets and think we should be doing this, we should be doing that - fixing potholes, improving the roads, stuff that matters to people."

His interest in highways was backed up at May's first council meeting, when Johnson told members he would double the budget for road markings by "repurposing Net Zero funding".

He also promised to "undeclare" the city's climate emergency.

Johnson points out the new markings and road surfaces around us, claiming to have found the money from "waste" under the last administration, enabling him to increase the budget from £41,000 to £82,000.

"People deserve a smart city centre, and not only have we done the surfaces and the white lines, we've washed all the paving down, we're getting rid of the graffiti, we're listening to local businesses."

Road markings across the district will now be reviewed.

Wakefield Council initially declared a climate emergency seven years ago, with a goal of becoming carbon neutral by 2030.

Johnson tabled a motion to axe the declaration in June, despite having backed it as a Conservative councillor in 2019.

"I'd actually say it's a very popular policy that we have got and we've been applauded for it.

"We're saving hundreds of thousands of pounds in this district to be able to then put back into things that residents and local people actually need."

Green Party councillor Kate Dodd, who opposed the motion, disagrees.

"To suggest this is not an emergency and not something that urgently needs to be tackled is frankly irresponsible."

In the run-up to the local elections one of the big issues was the regeneration of Wakefield city centre and the future of The Ridings Shopping Centre.

In February, the Labour-led authority agreed to buy the centre so they could demolish it. Four nearby tower blocks would also be knocked down.

At the time, Labour's deputy leader Jack Hemmingway said the government was providing £17.9m towards redeveloping the area, describing it as "a once in a generation opportunity to transform the city centre".

The move was to prove controversial with businesses in The Ridings and residents of the tower blocks opposed to the plan.

Ahead of the election, the Reform group hadn't reached a "settled view" as to what they thought should happen to the site.

Since May, the authority has said it will carry out further consultations on the proposals with residents.

Johnson says: "Why would you buy a shopping centre a week before an election? We've been left it and we're going to deliver big style because it shouldn't have happened in the lead-up to an election.

"It's only fair that the public of Wakefield get their voice heard on what they want to see in their own city centre.

"We need to make sure it makes financial sense and it's deliverable. We need to make sure that the next 40 years are a success.

"I do have ideas, but are my ideas any stronger than residents'? I'm a resident here, and I put forward what I think in the consultation."

The consultation is due back in the next few weeks and the council hopes to share the results in the autumn.

One of Reform's flagship policies nationally is to keep council tax rises to a minimum .

Leader Nigel Farage has pledged his party will "start to cut excessive expenditure" so it can raise council tax by less than other parties.

Reform in Wakefield have yet to set out their first budget and Johnson says he wants to make no promises, adding he needs to make sure "services are not cut" first.

"I would like to see council tax lower, but I don't want to be the politician that gives the lie that we're going to cut it by this; it will be lower if we can make things work without cutting services."

With this comment, Johnson has summed up the challenges for Wakefield - can Reform give the public what they want without making compromises? Time will tell.

articles.title: MP calls for transparency over Mildenhall drone factory protection
articles.summary: There are concerns about what protection is in place at a Ukrainian drone plant in the UK.
articles.body:
An MP has called on the government to be "as transparent as they can be" about protection for drone factories in the UK.

It comes after Russian former deputy foreign minister Andrei Fedorov told BBC Newsnight there might be a "semi-military" response against UK drone factories by "unknown sources" after the UK government shared blueprints for cruise missile components with Ukraine.

Shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy represents Mildenhall which is home to a new Ukrainian-owned factory, which can make 1,000 drones a month.

The Ministry for Defence (MoD) said it would not comment on specific security procedures.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham visited Ukraine on Monday, where he met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv.

The British government agreed to hand over blueprints for UK-made components for the Scalp missile, which is a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile - allowing Ukraine to produce the long-range weapon domestically.

A Kremlin spokesman, Dmitry Peskov, criticised the UK's decision to share the missile blueprints on Monday. Peskov said: "Britain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime. Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel to the fire," he added.

In response, Burnham said: "Who started the fire? That's the question, isn't it?"

The drone factory in Mildenhall was opened in February and is run by Ukrspecsystems, a Ukrainian firm.

At the time, it said it had repurposed a building in order to produce the unmanned aircraft as part of a £200m investment.

West Suffolk Conservative MP Timothy said: "It is not news that Russia targets British infrastructure, including military and industrial sites.

"MI5 has warned for years that so-called hybrid warfare methods are a threat to us and we must be prepared for them. "

Local politicians are also seeking reassurances.

Mildenhall Town Council's Mayor Russell Leaman said: "When a state like Russia says it may take retaliatory action and we have a large drone factory in Mildenhall, it's of concern.

"Day-to-day, I don't think it will affect too many people, but obviously there are some people that are anxious and worry. It would be nice to have some reassurance."

Asked if the town council had been contacted by the authorities to offer any reassurance, Leaman said it had not.

Shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge said a key issue was "strengthening cyber resilience", including using logins for systems and two-factor authenticators.

Cartlidge, Conservative MP for South Suffolk, said we must not "over interpret" Russian declarations as they had been happening since the start of the war in Ukraine and the annexation in Crimea.

"People do need to understand the threat - if they understand the threat more they are therefore more likely to accept that comes with more consequences like being more careful on cyber security and having to spend more of our taxes on the military," he added.

The drone factory is in the West Suffolk Council ward represented by Andy Neal from the West Suffolk Independent group. He questioned whether it had been naive for the location to be made public.

When the factory opened, the MoD said up to 500 jobs would be created. Neal said it would be a "massive" threat to the people working there and their families.

He also believed its proximity to RAF Mildenhall, home to the US Air Force (USAF) refuelling wing, would mean there would not be an aerial attack on the factory, but instead there could be some kind of "sabotage".

A USAF spokesperson said: "US Air Forces in Europe remain vigilant and ready to defend against any potential threats. We are committed to the safety of our airmen, families, mission partners and surrounding communities.

"We continue to work closely with our local law enforcement partners to ensure security measures are maintained."

The MoD said it would not comment on specific security procedures as this could benefit potential adversaries, but it said the security of defence assets was a top priority for the Labour government.

It added: "The first duty of government is national security. We take the security of our people, sites and local communities extremely seriously, and we continually review and strengthen our security arrangements.

"The public should be reassured that the UK and its allies remain vigilant against potential threats. We will not comment on specific security measures, but Russia should be in no doubt about the resolve of this government to stand against Russian aggression, in Ukraine and against the UK and our allies."

Ukrspecsystems has also been contacted for comment.

articles.title: India built bigger roads, flyovers and expressways. So why does rain still bring its cities to a standstill?
articles.summary: For years, India has been building bigger roads, wider highways, flyovers, expressways and new urban corridors. The country has invested heavily in im.
articles.body: For years, India has been building bigger roads, wider highways, flyovers, expressways and new urban corridors. The country has invested heavily in improving the way people move through its cities. Yet every monsoon brings back an uncomfortable question: why can a city with six-lane roads, elevated corridors and new expressways still be brought to its knees by a few hours of heavy rain? The answer lies in what lies beneath and around those roads — the drainage, natural water channels, wetlands and basic urban systems that have not kept pace with construction.Gurgaon's latest episode is a warningGurgaon offered a familiar but telling example this week. Around 70-75mm of rain in a relatively short spell on Monday was enough to flood major roads, trigger road cave-ins and turn routine journeys into hours-long ordeals. Parts of old Gurgaon, including Narsinghpur, Rajiv Chowk, IFFCO Chowk and Sohna Road, were badly affected. School buses, ambulances and commuters were caught in the water, while the administration advised people to work from home as the city struggled to restore normal traffic.The irony is hard to miss. Gurgaon has some of the country's most expensive commercial real estate and some of its busiest roads, yet moving people around during heavy rain remains a recurring problem. The city has repeatedly spent money on drain desilting, road repairs, pumping equipment and flood-control measures. Still, many of the same stretches return to the headlines every monsoon. The civic body is now planning water-injection wells at four flood-prone locations. Useful as such measures may be, they also raise a larger question: why are cities still responding to flooding largely after it happens instead of designing infrastructure that anticipates it?Delhi shows it isn't just a Gurgaon problemDelhi's experience this monsoon makes it clear that Gurgaon is not an isolated case. Safdarjung recorded 127mm of rain in the first seven days of August, while several parts of the capital saw much heavier short-duration spells later in the month. During one recent spell, Janakpuri received 67mm in less than five hours. Heavy rain disrupted traffic on the Delhi-Gurgaon Expressway and also affected airport operations. The problem was not simply the amount of rain. It was the speed at which the rain came down and the city's ability — or inability — to get rid of it.That distinction is becoming increasingly important. Indian cities are seeing intense bursts of rainfall that can dump large quantities of water over a small area within a few hours. A road may be perfectly capable of carrying thousands of vehicles every day, but that tells us almost nothing about how it will perform when several centimetres of rain fall in a short period. Once storm-water drains reach their capacity, roads, underpasses, service lanes and even parking areas start behaving like temporary drains. Traffic then becomes the first visible casualty.Even planned cities are failing the monsoon testChandigarh provides another uncomfortable example. The planned city received 72.4mm of rain in just two hours in one of the heaviest two-hour spells of this monsoon. Roads turned into streams, vehicles were stranded in waist-deep water, homes and shops were flooded and thousands of commuters were caught in traffic jams. A city that was designed with planning and zoning at its core was still struggling to cope with a concentrated burst of rainfall.That tells us something important. The problem is no longer simply about whether a city has enough roads or whether a particular junction needs a flyover. Decades of construction have covered large areas with concrete and asphalt, leaving less open ground for rainwater to seep into the soil. In many places, natural drains, wetlands and traditional water channels have been narrowed, blocked or built over. When the rain comes, there are simply fewer places for the water to go. A six-lane road can move traffic efficiently, but it cannot compensate for a storm-water system designed for a much smaller or very different city.We repair the road. We don't fix the systemThis is where India's familiar monsoon cycle begins. Heavy rain is followed by waterlogging, traffic jams, emergency pumping, drain cleaning, road repairs and promises of permanent solutions. Then the roads are patched, traffic resumes and the issue gradually disappears from public attention — until the next serious downpour. In Gurgaon, even a road costing around Rs 11.8 crore has faced flooding, while stretches such as MG Road, Ghata Road, Palam Vihar and Sheetla Mata Mandir Road have repeatedly suffered from waterlogging and damaged surfaces.There is also a problem with the way cities plan and manage infrastructure. The agency building a road may not be the one responsible for the drains alongside it. Another authority may control land development, while another responds when flooding occurs. Each part of the system can function reasonably well on its own and yet the city can fail as a whole. A flyover may remove a traffic bottleneck without addressing the drainage problem below it. An expressway may dramatically cut travel time on a normal day, but become another choke point when surrounding roads and underpasses are submerged.Monsoon has become a stress test for urban planningIndia does not necessarily need to respond to every traffic problem by building another road, flyover or elevated corridor. It needs cities that can continue functioning when extreme weather hits. That means identifying and protecting natural drainage channels, preserving wetlands, creating more permeable surfaces, increasing storm-water capacity and ensuring that roads are designed with proper gradients and outlets. It also means completing drain cleaning before the monsoon, rather than treating it as an emergency operation once water has already entered homes and roads.Technology can help too, but only if it is connected to action on the ground. Mumbai and Chennai have experimented with more sophisticated urban flood-warning systems, showing how rainfall forecasts, flood modelling and local alerts can help authorities respond before roads disappear under water. But a warning is useful only when there are pumps, clear drainage routes, traffic diversions and emergency teams ready to act on it.So the question after a major downpour needs to change. Instead of simply asking how much rain fell, cities should be asking how much rain their infrastructure was designed to handle, where the excess water was supposed to go and why critical roads became impassable. India's infrastructure progress cannot be measured only by kilometres of expressways, the number of flyovers or the width of its roads. If a few hours of rain can still strand schoolchildren, delay ambulances, disrupt airport operations and bring major business districts to a halt, the biggest infrastructure gap may not be the road above the ground. It may be the city underneath it.

articles.title: Hong Kong home prices fall for first time since March 2025
articles.summary: News News: Hong Kong’s property market had enjoyed a prolonged period of recovery, with residential prices benefiting from improving sentiment and steady demand..
articles.body: Hong Kong’s property market had enjoyed a prolonged period of recovery, with residential prices benefiting from improving sentiment and steady demand. But after months of gains, the market showed signs of losing some momentum in July, as buying activity came under pressure from developments in financial markets and tighter investment curbs in mainland China.Private home prices in Hong Kong fell 0.5 per cent in July, marking their first monthly decline since March 2025, according to data from the Rating and Valuation Department released on Thursday.The fall came after a revised 0.2 per cent increase in June. Despite the monthly decline, prices have risen 7.3 per cent during the first seven months of the year and are up 12.8 per cent from their trough in March 2025.Realtors expect the property market to undergo a short-term consolidation following its long period of gains. Buying demand has faced headwinds from a correction in stock markets and tighter curbs by China on outbound investment.Hong Kong’s property market, among the least affordable in the world, has nevertheless received support from positive market sentiment, buoyant stock markets and firm demand from a growing number of mainland Chinese professionals.An easing oversupply of homes has also supported the market.Residential prices in the Asian financial hub recorded their first annual increase last year after falling by nearly 30 per cent from their 2021 peak.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Drumcree: Parades Commission chair not quitting
articles.summary: Unionist parties and the Orange Order have called for the commission to stand down.
articles.body:
The chair of the Parades Commission has said she and her colleagues do not intend to resign.

Professor Evelyn Collins was speaking two days after a court case highlighted mistakes made by the commission in its ruling on last month's planned parade by the Orange Order to Drumcree church in Portadown.

Unionist parties and the Orange Order have called for the commission to stand down, but Prof Collins said they intend to stay in post.

"We will work hard to regain the trust of all sections of the community," she said.

Speaking to Good Morning Ulster , Collins added: "Rather than resign, the commissioners and I are very committed to fulfilling our responsibilities under the legislation, to completing our terms of office and to addressing and fixing the problems that have been identified."

She also said they "accept criticisms that have been made".

Nigel Dawson, Portadown District Master for the Orange Order, told The Nolan Show he was in "disbelief" listening to Collins on Good Morning Ulster.

Dawson called for Collins' resignation, adding that her position is "untenable" and that she "must take responsibility".

"[The Parades Commission] doesn't command the confidence of the loyal orders," he said.

"They don't command, I think, the confidence of the greater unionist community."

Dawson said the commission is "no longer fit for purpose", and that the reputations of those on the committee "are in "tatters".

"They cannot class themselves as independent," he added.

Dawson said he has contacted the Secretary of State, Sir Chris Bryant, to request a meeting.

First Minister Michelle O'Neill, who attended the Drumcree Community Centre on Wednesday and met residents who, said the community was "anxious by what they saw" on Tuesday.

She added that the "days of pushing any parades or any sort of negative experience again on any community here will not be acceptable or tolerated by anybody".

In a post on X, Democratic Unionist Party leader Gavin Robinson said that "any notion that the Parades Commission could muddle their way through was just blown out of the water by their Chair" on Good Morning Ulster.

He added that the secretary of state "will know that if resignations don't flow, he will have to act".

The Social Democratic and Labour Party leader Claire Hanna said the mistakes made by the commission "were a complete mess", but that it should not mean people "ignore the progress of the last 25 years".

"Residents have a right not to be intimidated."

The Orange Order has confirmed it intends to apply for another Drumcree parade in the coming days and a "significant date" in the calendar may be chosen for the parade.

Dawson said the Orange Order was agreeable to mediation with Garvaghy Road residents but questioned whether they wanted to engage in discussions.

A representative of a residents' group said there would be no point in discussions if the Orange Order had a "pre-determined outcome".

The current Commission was appointed from January 2024 on a three year term.

Professor Collins, a former chair of the Equality Commission, chairs a six-person panel. The others are Derek Wilson, a former banker, Billy Gamble, a former senior civil servant, Nicola Rountree, a barrister, Rachel Quigley, a solicitor and Pauline Leeson, a social worker.

According to the last annual report, the chair is paid between £50,000 and £55,000 while the other commissioners earn between £20,000 and £25,000.

The chair is expected to devote one to two days per week to the work of the Commission.

Commissioners are expected to devote approximately one day per week to commission business over the course of a year, with a proportionately greater commitment required April to August.

The member of the six-person commission who has faced the most public criticism is Billy Gamble.

He has been criticised over private comments he is alleged to have made about the Drumcree parade determination.

Collins (commission chair) said the comments were "out of line" but had no bearing on the decision-making process.

Asked if he should resign, the commission chair said: "That will be a matter for Billy Gamble."

In 1998, the Parades Commission ruled that the Orange Order should not march down Portadown's Garvaghy Road on the end leg of its annual march from Drumcree Church.

It was a move that ultimately led to a decades-long parading dispute, sparking some of the most serious public disorder in Northern Ireland's history.

Stand-offs continued in subsequent years as members of the Order walked to police barricades in protest at the restrictions. Protests were also held by residents living along the Garvaghy Road.

The High Court was told on Tuesday that the commission conceded the case last week and requested the court quash its determination before a full hearing.

The commission conceded a procedural error in how it dealt with the annual application for permission to walk along the Garvaghy Road.

Not all six members of the public authority had signed off on the final determination before it was issued last month.

Lawyers representing the local Orangeman claimed the commission's latest decision unlawfully breached his rights to freedom of belief, expression and peaceful assembly under the European Convention on Human Rights.

Lawyers for the applicant also argued that Garvaghy Road residents had refused talks with the Orange Order and the commission breached legislation by making it "a pre-requisite to a parade".

The Parades Commission said it "welcomes scrutiny and accountability".

The Grand Orange Lodge of Ireland said the ruling made "the position of the current commissioners untenable".

Breandan Mac Cionnaith of the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition said people "had pointed out their concerns, their worries" at a meeting with Michelle O'Neill on Wednesday.

"I think people also have to be realistic, it is 28 years since the last Orange march ever came down Garvaghy Road and it has already been said who wants to open that can of worms again?"

He said the Orange Order parade "finished" in 1998 and it "will not be repeated".

The secretary of state met the Parades Commission chair on Wednesday.

A Northern Ireland Office (NIO) spokesperson said Sir Chris Bryant expressed "serious concern over the issues highlighted" in the judgement during the meeting.

Sir Chris has asked for written assurances that the commission's decision-making processes are "fair and robust", that they act "independently and impartially" and that they have a plan to "enhance public confidence".

articles.title: 'The Toilet Kid': 9-year-old Washington boy collects toilet seats, tests their flushes and has turned his backyard into a giant toilet testing station
articles.summary: US News: A 9-year-old boy from Washington has become an unlikely social media sensation thanks to a childhood hobby that is anything but ordinary. Known online.
articles.body: A 9-year-old boy from Washington has become an unlikely social media sensation thanks to a childhood hobby that is anything but ordinary. Known online as “The Toilet Kid”, Damian has developed a fascination with toilets, toilet seats and household appliances, turning his interest into a hands-on backyard project. Rather than simply collecting unusual objects, Damian tests toilets to see how well they flush and has built a dedicated toilet test bench where he can put different models through their paces. Photos and videos of the young enthusiast show him posing alongside toilets and demonstrating his unusual setup, attracting attention from people fascinated by his passion. Damian is now planning to upgrade the testing bench so it can accommodate more of his growing toilet collection, giving his quirky hobby an even bigger stage.How 9-year-old Damian became 'The Toilet Kid'Damian's unusual interest in toilets has earned him the nickname “The Toilet Kid” online, where his videos and photographs have attracted a growing audience. His hobby centres on examining toilets and toilet seats and testing how they perform, particularly when it comes to flushing. What might appear to most people to be an ordinary household fixture has become an object of genuine curiosity for the young Washington boy. His enthusiasm also extends to other household appliances, giving his content a broader theme of exploring how everyday objects work. The appeal of Damian's videos comes partly from his obvious enthusiasm. Instead of treating toilets as something mundane, he approaches them with the curiosity normally associated with a child fascinated by cars, trains or machines.His backyard has become a toilet testing stationOne of the most unusual parts of Damian's hobby is the test bench he has set up in his backyard. The setup allows him to place toilets in position and conduct flushing experiments, giving him a dedicated space for examining different models. Images shared online show toilets positioned outdoors on a wooden structure, including a white toilet and another brown-coloured model connected to plumbing equipment. The setup has effectively transformed part of the backyard into a small testing area centred on toilets. For Damian, the bench provides more than a place to display his collection. It gives him somewhere to compare different toilets and observe how they perform when flushed, turning his fascination into a practical experiment.Damian is building a growing collectionThe toilet testing bench is also connected to Damian's growing collection. As he acquires more toilet-related items, he needs additional space to display and test them. He reportedly plans to upgrade the existing bench so that it can hold more toilets, allowing him to continue expanding the collection while keeping the testing area organised. His interest in toilet seats is particularly notable because these are usually overlooked as everyday household components. Damian instead treats them as objects worth collecting and examining. The collection and testing setup have therefore developed together, with the bench providing a practical way for him to explore the objects that interest him most.His hobby goes beyond simply collecting toiletsDamian's fascination is not limited to putting toilets on display. His interest in flushing gives the hobby an experimental element, as he can observe differences between models and see how effectively they perform. The approach reflects a broader curiosity about household technology and appliances. Children often develop intense interests in particular subjects, but Damian's hobby stands out because it involves full-sized household fixtures and a dedicated testing area. His willingness to share that interest publicly has also helped turn a private childhood pastime into something that thousands of people can discover online. The unusual combination of collecting, experimenting and documenting his activities has become the central appeal of “The Toilet Kid”.'The Toilet Kid' has gone viralDamian's story has attracted attention as it combines an ordinary household object with an extraordinarily specific childhood passion. Toilets are something almost everyone uses but rarely considers in detail, making a young boy who collects them and tests their flushing performance an inherently unexpected subject for viral content. His backyard setup adds another layer to the story because it turns the hobby into something physical and visual that can easily be captured in photographs and videos. The enthusiasm with which Damian approaches his collection also gives the story a wholesome quality. Rather than being presented simply as a joke, his interest shows how a child's curiosity can develop into a surprisingly detailed hobby.A bigger test bench could be nextDamian's plans suggest that “The Toilet Kid” is not finished building his unusual collection. He wants to upgrade his backyard test bench so it can accommodate more toilets, giving him additional room to continue his flushing experiments. A larger setup could allow him to display more of his collection while creating a more organised space for testing different models. For now, his backyard remains a modest but unusual testing station built around an interest that has captured the attention of people far beyond Washington. What began as a fascination with toilets has developed into a distinctive childhood hobby, complete with collecting, testing and documenting. As Damian continues expanding his setup, his followers will likely be watching to see what toilet joins the collection next.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Artemis II astronauts are set to receive America's highest spaceflight honour on August 28
articles.summary: US News: The four astronauts who flew NASA's Artemis II mission around the Moon are set to receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor, one of the highest d.
articles.body: The four astronauts who flew NASA's Artemis II mission around the Moon are set to receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor, one of the highest distinctions the United States awards for achievements in human spaceflight. According to NASA, President Donald J. Trump will present the medal to NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, along with Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen, during a ceremony at 11 a.m. EDT on Friday, August 28, at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston. The honour comes after the crew completed a roughly 10-day mission that launched in April 2026 and carried them around the Moon before returning safely to Earth. Artemis II marked the first crewed mission to travel beyond low Earth orbit since the Apollo era and sent humans farther from Earth than any previous crewed mission, making it a major milestone in NASA's return to deep-space exploration.Why Artemis II was such a significant missionArtemis II was the first crewed flight of NASA's Orion spacecraft and the first crewed mission in more than 50 years to travel beyond low Earth orbit. Wiseman served as commander, Glover as pilot, while Koch and Hansen served as mission specialists. The crew travelled around the Moon before returning to Earth, putting Orion's life-support systems, navigation, communications and other technologies through their first major crewed test in deep space. Hansen's participation also gave the mission an international significance. He became the first Canadian to travel to the Moon and the first non-American astronaut to fly on a mission to the lunar region. The mission concluded with the crew's splashdown on April 10, 2026, after roughly 10 days in space.Why so few astronauts have received the Congressional Space Medal of HonourThe Congressional Space Medal of Honour is awarded to astronauts whose achievements have made an exceptional contribution to the welfare of the nation and humanity. It is separate from NASA's own Distinguished Service Medal and is among the rarest major American honours specifically associated with human spaceflight. According to CBS News, only 30 astronauts had received the Congressional Space Medal of Honour before the Artemis II crew were selected as recipients. Previous honourees include some of the most famous names in American space exploration, including Neil Armstrong and John Glenn. The medal's rarity reflects the standard required for receiving it. It is not simply an award for completing a successful mission, but recognition reserved for extraordinary achievements and contributions to space exploration. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman is also expected to attend the August 28 ceremony alongside Trump and the Artemis II astronauts.What Artemis II proved for NASA's return to the MoonArtemis II was designed as a test of the systems and procedures NASA will need for later crewed lunar missions. Unlike Artemis I, which sent an uncrewed Orion spacecraft around the Moon in 2022, Artemis II carried people into deep space for the first time under the Artemis program The mission therefore provided NASA with experience operating a crewed spacecraft far beyond low Earth orbit, while also allowing astronauts to evaluate conditions that cannot be fully reproduced on Earth. The flight is part of NASA's wider Artemis program, which aims to return astronauts to the lunar surface and establish a longer-term human presence around and on the Moon. NASA also views the lunar program as preparation for eventual human missions to Mars. For the Artemis II crew, the August 28 ceremony will mark the formal recognition of a mission that reopened a chapter in human exploration that had been closed since the final Apollo flights more than half a century ago.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
