articles.title: US Justice Department and FBI seize domains claimed to be used by China-linked hacking group targeting NASA, Federal Reserve and more
articles.summary: Tech News News: The US Justice Department and the FBI have announced the seizure of internet domains linked to two hacking platforms allegedly used by a China state-s.
articles.body: The US Justice Department and the FBI have announced the seizure of internet domains linked to two hacking platforms allegedly used by a China state-sponsored cyber group to target critical infrastructure and sensitive networks. The platforms, known as QScan and QTRouter, were allegedly used to hide the origin of cyberattacks by routing malicious activity through compromised devices around the world. US authorities said the group's alleged victims included NASA, the Federal Reserve, the Department of Energy, the Department of Justice and the US Senate.FBI says platforms were used to hide the origin of attacksAccording to court documents, US authorities have linked the platforms to a group known as QTFY, which they say is employed by China-based Nanjing Xinjiuwei Network Technology Company. The Justice Department alleged that the group offered hacking services to paying customers, including China's Ministry of State Security and the People's Liberation Army.QScan allegedly scanned and automatically infected thousands of internet-connected devices, adding them to a network controlled through QTRouter.The compromised devices were then used to make malicious internet traffic appear to come from locations outside China, helping hackers conceal the origin of their activities, according to the Justice Department.“Today we announced the disruption of a global botnet and hacking platform used by Chinese state-sponsored hackers to target U.S. critical infrastructure,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “These tools were used by PRC cyber actors to hide the origin of their attacks.”Seized domains made QScan and QTRouter inoperable, DOJ saysThe Justice Department said the seized domains were hard-coded into the QScan and QTRouter malware and were needed for important functions, including communication and authentication. As a result, the court-authorized domain seizures made both platforms inoperable, according to the department.“State-sponsored malicious hackers preying on America’s critical infrastructure will be stopped and prosecuted,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said. “We are here to ensure security for the American people and will use every tool we have to keep that promise.”The latest action follows several other operations by US authorities against alleged China-sponsored hacking activity. In 2025, the FBI said it removed PlugX surveillance malware from more than 4,000 computers in the US that had been infected by the group known as Mustang Panda. In 2024, authorities said they disabled a large network of compromised internet-of-things devices linked to Flax Typhoon. The FBI also disrupted another botnet in 2023 that it said was used by Volt Typhoon to conceal cyber activity targeting critical infrastructure.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: In pictures: The dotty world of Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama
articles.summary: Kusama was known for creating extraordinary immersive worlds that delighted millions of visitors.
articles.body:
Using bright colours, shapes, patterns and reflections, Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama, who has died at the age of 97 , was known for creating extraordinary immersive worlds that delighted millions of people around the globe.

Kusama emerged as part of the pop art movement - and was among a select group of artists whose work became truly popular with a mass audience, attracting crowds to exhibitions from Tokyo to New York and London.

Her trademark polka dots covered entire galleries and giant sculptures, and she also used mirrors and lights to create the effect of shapes and patterns disappearing into infinity.

Actress Julia Fox (below) was among those at the opening of her exhibition in Melbourne, Australia in 2024.

Kusama said she saw hallucinations of dots and lights as a child, and used those visions in her art from the 1960s.

Kusama made a major global breakthrough after representing Japan at the Venice Biennale in the 1990s.

She is pictured inside one of her Infinity Mirror Rooms in Paris in 2001 above, and with fellow Japanese artist Yoko Ono in Sydney in 2000 below.

She had exhibitions at institutions including the Museum of Modern Art in New York, Tate Modern in London and the National Museum of Modern Art in Tokyo.

Visitors themselves applied more than 800,000 polka dot stickers to a white room (and their own faces) at the Smithsonian Institute's Hirshhorn Museum in Washington DC in 2017.

Kusama's 2012 retrospective at the Tate Modern was followed by an installation of her Infinity Mirror Rooms at the same venue from 2021, which drew huge audiences and was extended several times.

In 2023, a giant figure of Kusama was installed to tower over Louis Vuitton's flagship store on the Champs-Élysées in Paris.

Her giant figures, shapes and animals filled Manchester's Aviva Studios when the venue opened in 2023.

From Manchester to Melbourne - her spots were also a hit in the Australian city two years ago.

She had voluntarily lived in a psychiatric hospital for decades, and died in a Tokyo hospital earlier this month.

articles.title: Wyoming pizza shop gets fake $300 order for 18 pizzas, owner donates entire batch to hospital as former employee volunteers to deliver them to emergency room
articles.summary: US News: A pizza restaurant in Cheyenne, Wyoming, was left with 18 freshly made pizzas worth about $300 after a large order turned out to be fraudulent. L’Oste.
articles.body: A pizza restaurant in Cheyenne, Wyoming, was left with 18 freshly made pizzas worth about $300 after a large order turned out to be fraudulent. L’Osteria Mondello had prepared the pizzas after receiving a call from someone who reportedly said they were ordering food for a children’s wrestling club. The customer never arrived to collect the order, and when restaurant owner Dave Agovic called the number provided, the person who answered said they had not placed the order. Instead of throwing away the food or simply absorbing the loss, Agovic decided to donate the pizzas to the emergency room at Cheyenne Regional Medical Center. An unexpected helping hand then arrived when former restaurant employee Ryan Lemley volunteered to deliver the unwanted pizzas to hospital staff.$300 pizza order turned into a prankThe incident happened on August 14, 2026, when L’Osteria Mondello received an unusually large order for 18 pizzas. The caller reportedly told the restaurant that the food was intended for a children’s wrestling club, giving the staff a reason to believe it was a legitimate group order. The kitchen prepared the entire order, with the pizzas taking around 40 minutes to make. Once they were finished, the restaurant kept them warm above the ovens while waiting for the customer to arrive and collect them. Nobody showed up, however, and the situation became suspicious. Agovic eventually called the telephone number supplied with the order, only for the person who answered to say they had not ordered the pizzas. That convinced the restaurant that someone had used the number to place a fraudulent order.The restaurant was already handling a busy eveningThe fake order arrived during an especially hectic period for the restaurant. Agovic said the kitchen was simultaneously preparing another order for around 12 or 13 pizzas and a separate order for another seven or eight. That meant staff were dealing with more than 40 pizzas at roughly the same time. The restaurant became so busy that it temporarily stopped taking additional orders and warned customers that new orders could take between 1½ and 2 hours. The unexpected 18-pizza order therefore consumed significant kitchen time and ingredients at a moment when staff were already under pressure. Once the supposed customer failed to appear, the restaurant was left with a large amount of food that had been prepared specifically for an order that did not exist.Why the restaurant did not ask for payment upfrontAgovic said L’Osteria Mondello generally does not require customers to pay for orders in advance. His approach is based partly on trust, and he told Cowboy State Daily that a similar incident had happened only once before during his roughly 3½ years running the restaurant. The policy meant the restaurant had little protection against someone placing a large order without intending to collect it. The incident therefore cost the business not only the value of the pizzas but also the staff time and ingredients required to prepare them. Rather than immediately changing the restaurant’s approach, Agovic focused on finding a useful destination for the food that had already been made.Owner decides to donate all 18 pizzasWith the order abandoned, Agovic discussed the situation with his employees and suggested taking the pizzas to a hospital instead of allowing them to go to waste. The restaurant chose the emergency room at Cheyenne Regional Medical Center, turning what had started as a frustrating loss into an unexpected donation. The decision meant that the pizzas could still be eaten rather than discarded after the restaurant had spent time and money preparing them. The incident also gave the restaurant an opportunity to help people working in a demanding environment. Importantly, reports indicate that the pizzas were donated to emergency-room staff rather than specifically to patients, so the episode is best described as a donation to hospital workers.Former employee volunteers to deliver the pizzasThe hospital donation became possible with help from a former member of the restaurant team. Ryan Lemley, an 18-year-old who had worked at L’Osteria Mondello for more than two years, happened to stop by the restaurant while staff were deciding what to do with the pizzas. After hearing about the abandoned order, Lemley volunteered to take the food to the hospital. He delivered the pizzas to the emergency room at Cheyenne Regional Medical Center, ensuring that the restaurant did not have to throw away the entire order. Agovic later praised Lemley for stepping in and described him as his “hero that day”. His involvement added an unexpected second act of kindness to an incident that had initially been caused by someone else's prank.The pizzas found a new purpose at the hospitalThe 18 pizzas ultimately ended up with workers at the Cheyenne Regional Medical Center emergency room. What had been prepared for a supposed children's wrestling club instead became an unplanned meal for hospital staff. The episode illustrates how quickly the value of unwanted food can change when a business finds a practical way to redirect it. Rather than allowing the food to become waste, L’Osteria Mondello used an existing community connection to put the pizzas to use. The restaurant also shared the story publicly, helping the unusual incident spread beyond Cheyenne and attracting attention because of the positive response to the prank.The owner chose a positive response to the prankThe incident could have ended simply as a $300 loss for a small restaurant, but Agovic's decision changed the outcome. The restaurant still absorbed the cost of the ingredients and labour, while the person who placed the order remained unidentified in the available reporting. Yet the business chose not to let the prank determine what happened to the food. By donating the 18 pizzas and accepting help from a former employee, L’Osteria Mondello turned an attempted waste of food into a gesture towards hospital workers. The episode ultimately left the restaurant out of pocket, but it also created a story about trust, community and making the best of an unexpectedly bad situation.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Russian attacks on Ukraine leave several injured in multiple regions
articles.summary: Russia has attacked critical infrastructure in the Poltava, Sumy and Kherson regions, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Thursday, as the two cou...
articles.body:
Russia has attacked critical infrastructure in the Poltava, Sumy and Kherson regions, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Thursday, as the two countries continued their reciprocal airstrikes on targets deep in each other's territory.

Five people were injured in attacks on the Zaporizhzhya and Dnipropetrovsk regions, Zelensky said on social media. There was also damage caused by attacks in the Odessa region, he added.

Local authorities said that warehouses in Boryspil district east of Kiev caught fire following Russian attacks. At least two people had been injured, they said. Falling debris had also caused damage to several buildings in Kiev itself.

In the centre of the city of 3 million people, the military administration said a sports facility was damaged in the city centre. Pictures on social media showed a cloud of smoke near the Valeriy Lobanovskyi Stadium on the edge of the government district.

The Ukrainian air force said it had intercepted seven ballistic missiles. It also said an Oniks anti-ship missile had been shot down.

According to Ukrainian sources, about 86% of the drones used by the Russian military were intercepted.

Five Russian drones also briefly violated Moldova's airspace, Moldova's Defence Ministry in Chișinău said.

Ukraine in turn continued its attacks on warehouses belonging to Russian online retailers.

In the Ural region, a logistics centre of Ozon, Russia's second-largest online marketplace, was attacked by Ukrainian drones. The company said a distribution centre in Orenburg, near the Kazakh border, also had to be briefly evacuated due to a missile threat. However, there were no casualties or damage.

Ukraine has been defending itself against a Russian invasion for more than four and a half years. Kiev's counterstrikes have focussed on oil infrastructure, and more recently on Russian online retailers.
